chunks: Musa ibn al-Qasim from Ibn Abi Umayr from Hammad from al-Halabi from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said:

"The ritual of the one who combines Hajj and Umrah between Safa and Marwa is like the ritual of the Mufrid, and is not superior to it except by the accompanying sacrifice, and upon him is Tawaf around the House, and prayer of two rak'ahs behind the Maqam, and one Sa'i between Safa and Marwa, and Tawaf around the House after Hajj."

And he said: "Any man who combines Hajj and Umrah, it is not valid for him except that he drives the sacrifice, and he has marked it and tied the cord around its neck. And marking is that he pierces its hump with an iron tool until it bleeds. And if he does not drive the sacrifice, let him make it a Mut'ah."

His saying (peace be upon him): 'Any man who combines Hajj and Umrah' means in the Talbiyah of Ihram, because he needs to say 'If it is not a Hajj, then an Umrah'. And the difference between him and the Mutamatti' is that the Mutamatti' says this statement and intends Umrah before Hajj, then releases after that and enters Ihram for Hajj, so he becomes a Mutamatti'. And the Sa'iq (one who combines) says this statement and intends Hajj; if Hajj is not completed for him, he makes it an Umrah Mufradah. This meaning was narrated.

key_terms.الْمُتَمَتِّعِ: The Mutamatti' (one who performs Umrah then Hajj separately)
key_terms.الْمُفْرِدِ: The Mufrid (one who performs Hajj alone)

ai.seo_question: What are the differences between the Qarin, Mufrid, and Mutamatti' in Shia jurisprudence of Hajj?
ai.summary: This hadith from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam* clarifies the jurisprudence of *Qiran*, where the pilgrim combines Hajj and Umrah in a single Ihram, ruling that its core rituals mirror those of the *Mufrid* except for the obligatory sacrifice (*Hady*). It provides a precise legal distinction between the *Qarin* and the *Mutamatti'* based on the initial intention (*niyyah*) at the time of Ihram, a key differentiator in Shia fiqh. The text further details the physical marking of the sacrificial animal, emphasizing the tangible commitment required of the pilgrim.
